game_types.name: Respond under a rule
game_types.what_the_player_does: A stimulus appears; the player applies a rule they were given and responds.
game_types.boundary: The answer depends only on the stimulus in front of the player and the rule, not on material studied earlier.

rules.question: What competes with the correct response?

values.definition: Nothing competes with the correct response.
Items next to the target call for a different response (the flankers of a flanker display).
Another feature of the same item, which the player must ignore, calls for a different response (the word in Stroop).
Noise or a mask degrades the target.
An item shown just before the target favours one response.
The rule that was in force a moment ago still favours its own response.

rules.question: Does a cue come before the target?

values.definition: No cue comes before the target.
A cue says where the target will appear.
A cue says what can be won or lost on the trial.
A cue says which rule to apply.
A cue says only that the target is about to appear.
A cue says how likely it is that the player will have to respond or to hold back.
A cue gives a feature of the coming target, such as its color or shape.

rules.question: Is something held in mind to compare against?

values.definition: The response depends on the present stimulus alone.
The stimulus is compared with something the player keeps in memory, such as the item n steps back.

rules.question: Must the player ever hold back?

values.definition: The player responds on every trial.
The player makes no response on some trials (no-go trials).
The player stops a response already under way when a signal comes.
The player responds away from the stimulus, such as looking to the side opposite it.

rules.question: What does the rule ask about each stimulus?

values.definition: Say which category or feature the stimulus has.
Say whether a target is there.
Say whether the stimulus matches a reference or an earlier item.
Say where the stimulus is.
Produce an associated item, such as a verb for a noun.
Say which one the stimulus is, by name.
Say how many there are.

rules.question: Where does the rule come from?

values.definition: The player is told the rule.
A sequence or layout repeats and the player is not told.
The player works the rule out from right-or-wrong feedback.

rules.question: Does the rule change during play?

values.definition: The rule stays the same throughout.
The rule changes without warning and the player finds out from feedback.
The rule changes and a cue says which rule applies.

rules.question: How do the stimuli arrive?
rules.note: `continuous` means there are no trial boundaries (tracking, drawing through a display). A run of trials with no pause between them, as in N-Back, is `discrete_trials`.

values.definition: One trial at a time, each with its own start and end, whether or not there is a pause between them.
The stimulus runs continuously with no trial boundaries (tracking, drawing through a display).
Items follow one another rapidly at one place, faster than one response per item.

rules.question: How often is there a target?
rules.note: `every_trial` means the main response is called for on most or all trials; `rare_target` means the stimulus that calls for it is rare (Oddball, Continuous Performance). Go/No-Go is `every_trial` with `response_demand: withhold_on_some`.

values.definition: The main response is called for on most or all trials.
The stimulus that calls for the main response appears on a minority of trials.

game_types.name: Study, then be tested
game_types.what_the_player_does: The player takes material in, holds it over an interval, then shows what they kept.
game_types.boundary: There is material to keep and a later test of it, even when the interval is a second.

rules.question: How many study-test rounds?
rules.note: `one` means each set of material is studied once, however many trials there are. `repeated_lists` means the same material is studied again. Sternberg is `one`.

values.definition: Each set of material is studied once and tested once, however many sets there are.
Study and test repeat until the player reaches a set level of performance.
The same material is studied and tested again over several rounds.

rules.question: Is a judgment about one's own memory added?

values.definition: No judgment about the player's own memory is asked for.
After failing to recall an item, the player rates the chance of recognizing it later (feeling of knowing).
While studying, the player predicts how well each item will be remembered (judgment of learning).

rules.question: What fills the interval?

values.definition: The interval between study and test is unfilled.
An unrelated job fills the interval.
Another list to learn fills the interval.

rules.question: Are study and test separate?

values.definition: Study comes first and the test follows.
Each item is both a test of earlier items and new material to keep (continuous recognition).

rules.question: How long is it held?

values.definition: The material is held for minutes.
The material is held for seconds.
The test comes unannounced; the player did not know the material would be tested.
The material is held for hours or days.

rules.question: What is studied?

values.definition: Single items, such as words or pictures.
Pairs of items to be linked.
A sequence whose order must be kept.
Items together with where or how each was presented.

rules.question: What is the player told to remember?

values.definition: The player is told to remember everything presented.
A cue after each item or list says whether to remember it or forget it.

rules.question: What does the player do while studying?

values.definition: The player studies the material with no other job.
The player makes a judgment about each item, not knowing a test is coming.
The player judges whether each item describes themselves.

rules.question: What form does the test take?

values.definition: Recall given a cue, such as one member of a studied pair.
Pick the studied item from a set of alternatives.
Recall as much as possible, in any order.
Recall in the order of presentation.
Say whether each item was studied.
Say whether each item was studied and, if so, whether it is remembered or only known.
Say whether a display is the same as the one studied or has changed.
Say where or how each item was studied.

game_types.name: Choose for a payoff
game_types.what_the_player_does: The player picks an option, sees what it pays, and picks again.
game_types.boundary: No option is correct by instruction; the options differ in what they pay.

rules.question: Does a cue say which payoffs are in force?

values.definition: No cue says which payoffs are in force.
A cue on each trial says which payoffs are in force.

rules.question: Does what pays change?

values.definition: What each option pays stays the same throughout.
What each option pays changes gradually.
What the options pay is swapped at some point, without warning.

rules.question: What are the options?

values.definition: Several options whose payoffs are learned by trying them (decks, arms).
Pairs of symbols whose values are learned.
Two options whose payoffs are stated.
One option to keep taking until the player chooses to stop (pumping a balloon).

rules.question: How does the player learn what pays?

values.definition: The player learns what an option pays by choosing it and seeing the outcome.
The player is told what each option pays before choosing.

rules.question: What is traded against what?
rules.note: `explore_vs_exploit` is for options whose values the player must keep tracking (bandits). Iowa Gambling is `amount_vs_risk`: the decks differ in the size of the payoff and the risk of loss.

values.definition: A bigger reward against a bigger risk of loss.
A bigger reward against more effort.
Trying other options against staying with the best known one, where values must be tracked.
Learning which option pays most often.
A bigger reward against a longer wait.

game_types.name: Play against another player
game_types.what_the_player_does: The player makes a move whose payoff depends on what another player does.
game_types.boundary: Another player, real or said to be real, has a stake in the outcome.

rules.question: Can a player opt out?

values.definition: The player cannot leave the game.
The player can leave the game, usually at a cost, without the other player learning of it.

rules.question: In what order?

values.definition: The players move in turn and the second sees the first move.
The players move at the same time, without seeing the other's move.

rules.question: Who is the other player?

values.definition: A person, real or said to be real.
A computer, known by the player to be one.
A group of people.

rules.question: Who makes a move?

values.definition: Two players, each of whom makes a move.
More than two players make a move.

rules.question: Is the game played once or repeatedly?

values.definition: The game is played once with a given partner.
The game is played repeatedly with the same partner.

rules.question: Is what is sent changed on the way?

values.definition: What one player sends is what the other receives.
What one player sends is multiplied before the other receives it.

game_types.name: Solve a puzzle
game_types.what_the_player_does: The player works out an answer or a sequence of moves.
game_types.boundary: The answer has to be worked out; it cannot be read off the stimulus by a rule.

game_types.name: Make a movement
game_types.what_the_player_does: The player carries out or learns a movement pattern.
game_types.boundary: The movement itself is measured, not a choice it expresses.

game_types.name: Watch or listen
game_types.what_the_player_does: The player takes in a stream; the measure is the response to the stream itself.
game_types.boundary: No answer is scored against a correct one as a main measure.

rules.question: What is the player told to do while it runs?
rules.note: `attend` covers 'simply view' and 'listen'. `none` is for a stream the player is told to ignore or is given no instruction about (Mismatch Negativity).

values.definition: The player is told to attend to the stream; covers 'simply view' and 'listen'.
The player is told to ignore the stream or is given no instruction about it.
The player is told to change their emotional response to the stream.
The player is given a job that does not ask about the property being studied.

rules.question: Is anything asked afterwards?

values.definition: A rating, such as of fear, expectancy or pleasantness.
A question about what was read or heard.
Nothing is asked afterwards.
A judgment about the content, such as how strongly one thing causes another.

game_types.name: Find the way
game_types.what_the_player_does: The player moves through a space to reach a goal.
game_types.boundary: The path through the space is the measure.

game_types.name: Report on yourself
game_types.what_the_player_does: The player reports an internal state, a timing, or a memory of their own.
game_types.boundary: No answer can be checked against a correct one.

game_types.name: Hold a state
game_types.what_the_player_does: The player keeps a bodily or mental state as instructed while the recording runs.
game_types.boundary: Nothing is presented that calls for a response and nothing is reported; holding the state is the whole job (rest, fixation).

values.definition: The player tries because they were asked to; nothing is won or lost.
Obtaining a reward or avoiding a loss is what the game is about.
A reward or loss is attached to performing well at a game that is about something else.
Something pleasant or unpleasant is delivered whatever the player does.
The instruction puts one of speed or accuracy first. The ordinary 'as fast and as accurately as you can' is `instructions_only`.

motivators.question: Can the player gain, lose, or both?

values.definition: The player can only gain.
The player can only lose or receive something unpleasant.
The player can gain and can lose.
The option the player chooses.
How fast or how accurately the player responds.
The player's move together with another player's move.
Nothing the player does; the outcome is delivered regardless.
Money.
Points with no stated money value.
Food or drink.
Approval, disapproval or another social outcome.
An unpleasant stimulus, such as a shock or a loud noise.
Effort the player must spend.
A signal of right or wrong, or of win or loss, with nothing behind it.
The outcome is delivered or paid.
The player is asked to choose as if the outcome were real.

phases.definition: The phase in which a relation is first learned.
The learned relation is no longer in force: the cue comes without its outcome.
What was learned is tested on new material or under new conditions.
An outcome is made less valuable before responding is tested.
A later phase that measures what was learned, with no further learning intended.

combinations.definition: The second game's stimulus follows the first's so closely that the two responses overlap.
The second game runs for the whole of the main game (holding fixation, a concurrent load).
Trials of the two games alternate or are mixed.
The second game is placed inside each trial or between the phases of the main game.
The outcome of one game is the starting point of the next.

settings.definition: Time between study and test, or sample and probe.
Time from one stimulus onset to the next (prime to target, cue to target, task 1 to task 2).
How long a stimulus is shown.
Size of a reward, loss, endowment or stake.
Length of a block or run.
Number of items in a display, memory set or option set.
Response options or choice alternatives.
Number of items in a studied list or sequence.
Trials per block or in total.
How often the target or rare item appears.
Target-distractor or lure-target similarity.
Time allowed to respond.
How many times a list or sequence is presented.
Blank time between two stimuli.
Targets per display or stream.
Chance an option pays off.
Contrast, loudness, coherence, signal-to-noise, noise density.
Items per second in a stream.
Share of congruent or valid or related trials (cue validity, relatedness proportion).
Share of feedback that is correct.
Time until a reward or outcome is delivered.
Distance from fixation.
Distance between items or sources.
Length of the whole session, or number of sessions.
Distractors per display.
Rotation or viewing angle.
Number of relational rules to integrate.
